newsitem.title: BANGLADESH: Bangladesh opposition demands release of leaders.
newsitem.headline: Bangladesh opposition demands release of leaders.

text.p: Bangladesh's main opposition leader Begum Khaleda Zia lashed out out on Thursday against the arrest of four of her party leaders and warned that she might launch a "relentless movement" against the government.
"This (arrest) is a naked expression of the government's fascist character," Khaleda told a meeting of her Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP) in Dhaka.
"We might be forced to launch a relentless movement...unless the detained leaders were freed," she said. "I call upon the government to behave democratically and refrain from repression."
In a pre-dawn swoop, police on Thursday arrested former ministers Khandaker Mosharraf Hossain, Abdul Mannan and Goyeswar Roy, and former Mayor of Dhaka, Mirza Abbas.
Police also raided the house of former minister Sadek Hossain Khoka but he managed to escape, his family said.

Police detained at least 10 BNP protesters during two rounds of clashes on Dhaka's streets following the arrests. The protesters attacked police with stones and damaged at least a dozen vehicles, witnesses said.
BNP's Secretary-General Abdul Mannan Bhuiyan said many party stalwarts had been in hiding to escape arrest.

The raids followed the BNP's call on Wednesday for a countrywide general strike on Sunday, a working day in mainly Moslem Bangladesh, in an attempt to topple the government of Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina.
"We can't give them any more time. They have proved more than inefficient in running the country," Zia told a party rally in Dhaka on Wednesday.
A relative of Khandaker Mosharraf Hossain, former energy minister, said: "Hundreds of police in uniform and civil dress stormed our house around 5 a.m. and just asked him to follow them."
A nephew of Abdul Mannan, former textile and civil aviation minister, added: "They produced no warrants and explained nothing."
Police said the former ministers were picked up by detectives but would not say on what charges.
Political analysts were divided on the possible impact of the arrests.
Some said they believed the "hard line" taken by Hasina's government was necessary to ensure political stability. Others said Hasina should have waited for public reaction to the BNP's strike call.
Khaleda branded Hasina's government "shamelessly pro-Indian", and said it had conspired to "let the big hegemonist power enhance its influence on the small neighbour".
"We can no longer cooperate with this government or keep silent when national interests are at stake," Khaleda told cheering supporters.
Khaleda also attacked Hasina's handling of the economy.
Hasina took office last June. The strike is the first major challenge faced by the eight-month-old government.
